title: The monsoon wait
hook: four months of rain; nothing to do

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sugriva and Vali, two brothers split by a sealed cave, and the arrow from behind the trees. Your line was choose a side carefully. Did you hear the other side once? Day fifty-six.

Look at this week. It started with a faked cry in the forest. Then a line in the dust, a beggar at the door, a flying chariot, an old bird who fought and fell. Rama broke. Shabari fed him berries. Two monkey brothers, one arrow, and a new king on the throne of Kishkindha. Everything is finally ready. Rama has an army. Sugriva has promised to search the whole world for Sita. Go, go, go. And then it starts to rain. Not a shower. The monsoon. And the whole story, after a week of running, has to sit down and wait four months.
screen: `A WEEK OF RUNNING.` → `AN ARMY, FINALLY.` → `THEN IT RAINS.`

segments.voice: In the rainy season, in ancient India, nobody traveled. Roads turned to mud, rivers flooded, armies stayed home. Sugriva tells Rama they'll start the search when the rains end. So Rama and Lakshmana wait in a cave on a mountainside, watching the storm. And here Valmiki does something remarkable. In the middle of an adventure story, he stops and writes page after page about rain. The clouds, heavy and dark, lowering over the hills. Peacocks dancing. Rivers running brown and fast. Frogs waking up. Lightning in the clouds. The whole earth drinking. It's some of the most loved nature poetry in Sanskrit. And it's told through the eyes of a man who is miserable. Every beautiful thing reminds Rama of Sita. The rain is gorgeous and he can't stand it. That's what waiting feels like, isn't it? The world keeps being beautiful while you're stuck. Lakshmana, again, is the steady one. He tells his brother, in effect: this is the season for waiting. When it turns, we move. Four months of rain, and the Ramayana doesn't skip it. Here's why that matters. Many Hindus still keep this season, chaturmas, the four months of the monsoon, as a time to slow down: holy wanderers stay in one place, some people take on a small vow or a simpler diet, and weddings often wait. The waiting isn't wasted. It's part of the calendar. A story about a hero could have jumped straight to the search. This one makes him sit in the rain.
screen: `NOBODY TRAVELS IN THE RAINS.` · `VALMIKI STOPS TO PAINT THE STORM.` · `BEAUTIFUL, AND RAMA CAN'T BEAR IT.` · `CHATURMAS: FOUR MONTHS OF WAITING.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your breath find its own pace. Think of something you're waiting for right now. A result, a reply, a person, a season of life to end. Notice how waiting feels in your body: tight chest, restless hands, whatever it is. Now, the way Valmiki does, look around you, or listen. What's here while you wait? A sound. A light. Your own breath. You don't have to like the waiting. Just let it be a season, not a prison, for two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The monsoon wait. Four months of rain, a hero who can't move, and some of the most beautiful poetry in the story.
Your line: waiting is a season. Today, while you wait for something, notice one beautiful thing you'd have missed if you weren't stuck. That's the week. Tomorrow the rain stops. Day fifty-six.

howItsDone: Many Hindus observe chaturmas, the four months of the monsoon, as a slower, more devotional season: renunciates stay in one place, some families take small vows or simplify their food, and many weddings are held before or after it.

original.note: Sanskrit: rain, and the rainy season. The monsoon months in the old six-season calendar.
